source.sourceQuote: Whatever helmet you decide on, keep it securely fastened on your head when you ride.

question: You are starting a ride at dusk that will finish after dark. What does the manual say about tinted eye protection?
choices: It should not be worn when little outside light is available
It should be worn whenever headlights are in use
It is preferred at night because it cuts oncoming headlight glare
It is acceptable at night if it is scratch-free
explanation: The manual states that tinted eye protection should not be worn when little outside light is available. A tint that is comfortable in daylight removes light you need once the sun is down, so a clear shield or clear goggles is the dusk-to-dark choice.
choiceExplanations: The rule is tied to available light, and it points the other way — tint comes off as light drops.
The manual gives no glare-reduction exception for night riding.
Being free of scratches is a separate requirement and does not make tint suitable in low light.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: Tinted eye protection should not be worn when little outside light is available.

question: What does a faceshield protect that goggles do not?
choices: The rest of your face, not just your eyes
Your hearing from engine and wind noise
Your neck from sunburn
Your eyes from watering in the wind
explanation: The manual draws the line clearly: a plastic impact-resistant faceshield can help protect your whole face in a crash, while goggles protect your eyes but will not protect the rest of your face like a faceshield does. Both also shield you from wind, dust, dirt, rain, insects and pebbles.
choiceExplanations: Hearing is protected by hearing protection, which the manual treats as its own item.
Sun protection for an exposed neck is discussed under travelling with cargo, not eye protection.
Goggles do protect the eyes from wind; that is not the difference between the two.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: Goggles protect your eyes, though they won't protect the rest of your face like a faceshield does.

question: What does the manual say about boots or shoes for riding?
choices: They should be high and sturdy enough to cover your ankles and give them support
Any closed-toe shoe is adequate for street riding
Heels should be tall enough to hook on the footrests
Laces should be left long so boots can be removed quickly
explanation: Boots or shoes should be high and sturdy enough to cover your ankles and give them support, with hard, durable, slip-resistant soles and short heels that will not catch on rough surfaces. Laces get tucked in so they cannot catch on the motorcycle.
choiceExplanations: Coverage and ankle support are the stated requirements, which a low closed-toe shoe does not meet.
The manual says to keep heels short so they do not catch on rough surfaces.
Laces should be tucked in so they will not catch on the motorcycle.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: Boots or shoes should be high and sturdy enough to cover your ankles and give them support.

question: Which material does the manual say offers the most protection in riding clothing?
choices: Leather
Denim
Nylon mesh
Cotton canvas
explanation: The manual states that leather offers the most protection, and adds that sturdy synthetic material provides a lot of protection as well. Either way, jacket and pants should cover the arms and legs completely and fit snugly enough to keep from flapping in the wind.
choiceExplanations: Denim is not named; the manual ranks leather first and sturdy synthetics close behind.
Mesh is not the protective ranking the manual gives, though synthetics can provide a lot of protection.
Cotton canvas is not identified as a protective riding material.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: Leather offers the most protection.

question: Why does the manual recommend wearing a jacket even in warm weather?
choices: To prevent dehydration
To satisfy state helmet law
To reduce wind noise
To make the bike easier to handle
explanation: The manual advises wearing a jacket even in warm weather to prevent dehydration, noting that many jackets are designed to protect without overheating you on summer days. Clothing also protects from heat, cold, debris and the hot and moving parts of the motorcycle.
choiceExplanations: Helmet law concerns head protection; it says nothing about jackets.
Wind noise is handled by hearing protection, not by a jacket.
Clothing does not change how the motorcycle handles.

source.sourceQuote: Jacket and pants should cover arms and legs completely.

question: How does the manual describe a motorcycle that fits you?
choices: Your feet reach the ground while seated and the controls are easy to operate
You can hold it upright with one hand while seated
The seat height is at least 32 inches
It weighs less than 400 pounds
explanation: The manual's fit test has two parts: your feet should reach the ground while you are seated on the motorcycle, and the controls should be easy to operate. It adds that smaller motorcycles are usually easier for beginners to operate.
choiceExplanations: No one-hand test appears in the manual's fit description.
The manual gives no seat-height figure; never assume a number it does not state.
No weight limit is given as a measure of fit.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: Your feet should reach the ground while you are seated on the motorcycle, and the controls should be easy to operate.

question: Which of these is NOT listed as minimum equipment for a street-legal motorcycle?
choices: A tachometer
Turn signals
Two mirrors
Front and rear brakes
explanation: The manual's minimum list for a street-legal motorcycle is a headlight, taillight and brake light; front and rear brakes; turn signals; a horn; and two mirrors. A tachometer is not among them.
choiceExplanations: Turn signals are on the manual's minimum equipment list.
Two mirrors are on the minimum equipment list.
Front and rear brakes are on the minimum equipment list.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: Front and rear brakes. • Turn signals. • Horn. • Two mirrors.

question: What does the manual say about the riders involved in more than half of all crashes?
choices: They have under five months of experience on that particular motorcycle
They have been riding for more than ten years
They are riding without a valid endorsement
They are riding machines with engines larger than 750cc
explanation: The manual states that more than half of all crashes involve riders with less than five months of experience on their motorcycle. The measure is experience on that particular machine, which is why it warns to ride extra carefully on any motorcycle that is new or unfamiliar to you.
choiceExplanations: Long experience is not what the statistic describes; recent unfamiliarity is.
The manual ties the figure to experience on the machine, not to licensing status.
No engine size appears anywhere in the statistic.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: More than half of all crashes involve riders with less than five months of experience on their motorcycle.

question: You borrow a friend's motorcycle. What does the manual say to do before riding it in traffic?
choices: Get familiar with it away from traffic and locate every control without looking
Ride it briefly in traffic at low speed to learn its handling
Adjust the suspension to your own weight before moving it
Nothing special, provided you already hold an endorsement
explanation: The manual says that if you borrow a motorcycle, get familiar with it away from traffic, and to find the turn signals, horn, headlight switch, fuel-supply valve and engine cut-off switch and operate them without having to look. Riding an unfamiliar motorcycle adds risk, and most crashes involve riders with under five months on their machine.
choiceExplanations: Learning an unfamiliar bike in traffic is the exact risk the manual tells you to remove first.
Suspension adjustment is advised for carrying loads or passengers, not as the borrowing step.
Holding an endorsement does not remove the unfamiliarity risk the manual warns about.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: If you borrow a motorcycle, get familiar with it away from traffic.

question: How often does the manual say a pre-ride inspection should be done?
choices: Before every ride
Once a week
Once a month
Before long trips only
explanation: A pre-ride inspection only takes a few minutes and should be done before every ride to prevent problems. The manual compares it to checking the weather forecast — routine and automatic — because a minor failure that merely inconveniences a driver can put a rider on the road surface.
choiceExplanations: Weekly is the stated interval for brake fluid and coolant, not for the whole inspection.
A monthly interval appears nowhere; the inspection belongs to every ride.
The manual applies it to every ride, not only to long ones.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: A pre-ride inspection only takes a few minutes and should be done before every ride to prevent problems.

question: T-CLOCS is the manual's reminder for what?
choices: The pre-ride inspection of the motorcycle
The four steps of a turn
The three-step SEE strategy
The staggered formation used in group riding
explanation: T-CLOCS is the MSF's pre-ride inspection reminder, and the manual says a T-CLOCS inspection should be conducted before every ride. The letters stand for Tires and wheels, Controls, Lights and electrics, Oil and other fluids, Chassis, and Stands.
choiceExplanations: The four steps of a turn are SLOW, LOOK, PRESS and ROLL.
SEE stands for Search, Evaluate and Execute, a separate strategy.
Staggered formation is a group-riding spacing pattern with no checklist acronym.

source.sourceQuote: A T-CLOCS inspection should be conducted before every ride

question: During the controls check, what should the throttle do when you release it?
choices: Snap back to fully closed
Stay where you left it until you close it by hand
Return slowly to about a quarter open
Hold engine speed steady at idle plus 1,000 rpm
explanation: Under C for Controls, the manual says to make sure the clutch and throttle operate smoothly, and that the throttle should snap back to fully closed when released. A throttle that does not is the same fault that later appears as the 'stuck throttle' emergency.
choiceExplanations: A throttle that holds its position is a stuck throttle, which the manual treats as an emergency.
Partial return is a fault, not the expected behaviour.
No such rpm behaviour is described; the check is simply that the throttle closes fully.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: The throttle should snap back to fully closed when released.

question: Why does the manual tell you to clean and adjust mirrors before starting out?
choices: It is difficult to ride with one hand while you try to adjust a mirror
Mirrors cannot be adjusted once the engine is warm
Adjusting mirrors while moving is illegal
A moving motorcycle's vibration prevents accurate adjustment
explanation: The manual's reason is practical: clean and adjust mirrors before starting, because it is difficult to ride with one hand while you try to adjust a mirror. Each mirror should be set so you can see the lane behind and the lane next to you — the road behind and to the side is what matters, not your own shoulder.
choiceExplanations: Engine temperature has nothing to do with mirror adjustment.
The manual gives a practical reason, not a legal one.
Vibration is not the reason given; riding one-handed is.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: Adjust each mirror so you can see the lane behind and the lane next to you.

question: What assumption does the manual say a rider must make about other drivers?
choices: You cannot be sure they will see you or yield the right of way
They will see you if your headlight is on
They will yield once eye contact is made
They will behave predictably in daylight
explanation: The manual is explicit: as a rider you cannot be sure that other operators will see you or yield the right of way. Everything else in the book — conspicuity, space cushion, SEE, covering the controls — is built on that assumption rather than on other people's good behaviour.
choiceExplanations: A headlight makes you twice as likely to be noticed during the day, but it is not a guarantee.
The manual says never to count on eye contact — a driver can look straight at you and not see you.
Daylight is when most crashes occur; it does not make other drivers predictable.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: As a rider you can't be sure that other operators will see you or yield the right of way.

question: A driver runs a yellow light turning red and collides with you as you pull out on green. How does the manual frame responsibility?
choices: It was the driver's responsibility to stop and your responsibility to look before moving out
Responsibility rests entirely with the driver who ran the light
Responsibility rests with you, because you entered the intersection
It is an accident — an unforeseen event without fault
explanation: This is the manual's own example. It concludes that it was the driver's responsibility to stop, and it was your responsibility to look before moving out. Someone else may start the chain of events, but that does not leave any of us free of our responsibility to reduce risk — and blame does not matter when someone is injured.
choiceExplanations: The manual refuses to place all responsibility on the other party, even when they broke the rule.
The manual does not shift the whole burden to the rider either; both had a duty.
The manual expressly rejects calling traffic crashes accidents, since they rarely occur without fault.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: Blame doesn't matter when someone is injured in a crash.

question: How far ahead does the manual say to search your path of travel?
choices: 12 seconds
4 seconds
2 seconds
20 seconds
explanation: Among the things that lessen your chances of a crash, the manual lists searching your path of travel 12 seconds ahead. That long look gives you time to prepare for a situation before it becomes urgent, while the 4-second and 2-second distances handle what is already close.
choiceExplanations: Four seconds is the immediate or urgent path, not the long search distance.
Two seconds is the minimum following distance, a different measurement.
Twenty seconds is not a figure the manual uses.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: Search your path of travel 12 seconds ahead.

question: A rider scans only as far ahead as the vehicle directly in front. Which lead time are they missing?
choices: The 12-second search of the path of travel
The 2-second following distance
The half-second reaction allowance
The 30-second route plan
explanation: The manual describes three lead times: at least a 2-second following distance, a 4-second immediate path, and a search out to an area it would take about 12 seconds to reach. A rider watching only the vehicle ahead has the short gap covered and has lost the 12-second look that would let them prepare before a problem becomes urgent.
choiceExplanations: Watching the vehicle directly ahead is roughly the 2-second gap; that is the part they are doing.
No half-second reaction allowance is defined in the manual.
There is no 30-second figure in the manual's lead times.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: Search your path of travel 12 seconds ahead.

question: Which of these does the manual list as a way to lessen your chances of a crash?
choices: Communicate your intentions with signals, brake light and lane position
Ride slightly above the flow of traffic to stay ahead of it
Stay in the centre of a lane at all times
Rely on eye contact to confirm a driver has seen you
explanation: The manual's list is: be visible, communicate your intentions, maintain an adequate space cushion, search your path of travel 12 seconds ahead, identify and separate hazards, and be prepared to act. Communicating intentions means using the proper signals, brake light and lane position.
choiceExplanations: Riding above the traffic flow is nowhere recommended; speed is not listed as a safety measure.
Lane position should change as traffic situations change, not stay fixed in the centre.
The manual says never count on eye contact — a driver can look at you and still not see you.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: Communicate your intentions - use the proper signals, brake light and lane position.

question: What does the manual mean by 'be visible'?
choices: Wear proper clothing, use your headlight, and ride in the best lane position to see and be seen
Ride only during daylight hours
Stay directly beside other vehicles so drivers can see you
Use your horn continuously in traffic
explanation: Under 'be visible' the manual names three things together: wear proper clothing, use your headlight, and ride in the best lane position to see and be seen. Visibility is something you arrange, not something you hope other drivers supply.
choiceExplanations: Daylight is when most crashes occur; visibility is about gear, lights and position, not time of day.
Riding alongside other vehicles puts you in blind spots and blocks your escape route.
The horn is for getting attention in specific situations, and is not as loud as a car's.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: Be visible - wear proper clothing, use your headlight, ride in the best lane position to see and be seen.

question: Where should your knees be while riding?
choices: Against the gas tank
Spread wide for balance
Tucked behind the footrests
Resting on the engine cases
explanation: The manual says to keep your knees against the gas tank to help you keep your balance as the motorcycle turns. That contact point, together with feet firmly on the footrests, is what lets your lower body hold position while your hands work the controls.
choiceExplanations: Spreading the knees removes the contact that helps hold you steady as the motorcycle turns.
Knees cannot reach behind the footrests, and feet belong firmly on the footrests themselves.
Resting on hot engine cases is neither possible for balance nor safe.

question: How far forward should you sit on the seat?
choices: Far enough forward that your arms are slightly bent on the handgrips
As far back as the seat allows, for comfort
Far enough forward that your arms are straight
Directly over the rear axle
explanation: The manual says to sit far enough forward so that your arms are slightly bent when you hold the handgrips, because bending your arms permits you to press on the handlebars without having to reach too far. Pressing the handgrip is exactly how you make the motorcycle lean and turn.
choiceExplanations: Sitting far back forces you to reach, which the manual's seating rule is written to avoid.
Straight arms prevent you pressing on the handlebars, which is how the motorcycle is steered.
Load placement relates to the rear axle; rider position is set by arm bend at the handgrips.

question: Why does the manual warn against letting your toes point downward?
choices: They may get caught between the road and the footrests
It reduces the grip of the rear brake pedal
It shifts weight too far back on the motorcycle
It makes the clutch harder to feather
explanation: The manual warns that if your toes point downward they may get caught between the road and the footrests. Feet stay firmly on the footrests, near the controls, and are never dragged — a foot catching on something can injure you and cost you control.
choiceExplanations: Rear brake grip is not affected by toe angle; the hazard is contact with the road.
Toe angle does not meaningfully change weight distribution.
The clutch is a hand lever on most motorcycles and is unrelated to foot position.

question: Where is the gearshift lever and how is it operated?
choices: In front of the left footrest, operated by the left foot
In front of the right footrest, operated by the right foot
On the left handlebar, operated by hand
Behind the left footrest, operated by the heel
explanation: The manual states that the gearshift lever is located in front of the left footrest and is operated by the left foot. Lift and release to shift up a gear; press down and release to shift down. Each lift or press changes exactly one gear.
choiceExplanations: The right foot works the rear brake pedal, not the gearshift.
The left hand works the clutch lever; shifting is a foot control.
The lever sits in front of the footrest and is lifted or pressed with the toe.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c

question: To shift up to a higher gear, what do you do with the shift lever?
choices: Position your foot under it, then lift and release
Press it down and release
Hold it up until the next gear engages
Press it down twice in quick succession
explanation: The manual says that to shift up to a higher gear you position your foot under the shift lever and lift and release. Spring loading returns the lever to centre so the mechanism resets for the next shift. The full upshift is a three-step process: roll off the throttle as you squeeze the clutch, lift the lever firmly, then smoothly ease out the clutch and adjust the throttle.
choiceExplanations: Pressing down and releasing is the downshift, not the upshift.
The lever is spring-loaded and returns to centre; holding it does nothing further.
Each press changes one gear down, so two presses would drop two gears.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c

question: What happens if you shift into a lower gear while still travelling too fast?
choices: The motorcycle will lurch and the rear wheel may skid
The engine will stall immediately
The transmission will refuse to select the gear
The front wheel will lift
explanation: The manual warns to make certain you are riding slowly enough when you shift into a lower gear, because if not, the motorcycle will lurch and the rear wheel may skid. A sudden change in power to the rear wheel is a skid risk, which is why smooth clutch release matters most on downshifts.
choiceExplanations: A stall is not what the manual describes; the problem is a lurch and possible rear-wheel skid.
The gear does engage — that is precisely why the lurch happens.
The manual attributes no front-wheel lift to downshifting too early.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Basic Vehicle Control

question: You are riding downhill and need a lower gear. What does the manual say you may need to do first?
choices: Use the brakes to slow sufficiently before downshifting safely
Accelerate briefly to match engine speed
Shift two gears at once to compensate for the slope
Pull in the clutch and coast until the hill flattens
explanation: The manual states that when riding downhill or shifting into first gear you may need to use the brakes to slow sufficiently before downshifting safely. Gravity is adding speed, so the brakes do the work the closed throttle would otherwise do before the lower gear is engaged.
choiceExplanations: Accelerating increases the speed mismatch the downshift is already struggling with.
Shifting through several gears at once is possible but does not solve being too fast for the gear.
Coasting with the clutch in removes engine braking exactly where a downhill needs it.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Basic Vehicle Control
source.sourceQuote: Make certain you are riding slowly enough when you shift into a lower gear.

question: What does the manual call the slowing effect produced by shifting to a lower gear?
choices: Engine braking
Compression locking
Linked braking
Trail braking
explanation: The manual states that shifting to a lower gear causes an effect similar to using the brakes, and that this is known as engine braking. To use it, shift down one gear at a time and ease out the clutch lever through the friction zone between downshifts.
choiceExplanations: Compression locking is not a term the manual uses.
Linked braking is a hydraulic system connecting the front and rear brakes.
Trail braking does not appear in the manual.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Basic Vehicle Control
source.sourceQuote: Shifting to a lower gear causes an effect similar to using the brakes. This is known as engine braking.

question: A rider slowing for a junction shifts down one gear at a time, easing the clutch out between shifts. What are they using?
choices: Engine braking
Counterbalancing
Integrated braking
The friction-zone launch technique
explanation: This is the manual's description of engine braking: shift down one gear at a time and ease out the clutch lever through the friction zone between each downshift, staying in the friction zone until engine speed stabilises. It supplements the brakes rather than replacing them.
choiceExplanations: Counterbalancing is a body-position technique for slow, tight turns.
Integrated braking is a hydraulic system that applies partial front brake with the rear.
No such technique is described; the friction zone is used here as part of engine braking.

question: How often does the manual say to use both brakes?
choices: Every time you slow or stop
Only in emergency stops
Only when the road surface is dry
Only when carrying a passenger or cargo
explanation: The manual says to always use both brakes every time you slow or stop, and explains why: using both brakes for even normal stops will permit you to develop the proper skill of using both brakes properly in an emergency. The emergency is not the moment to try the front brake for the first time.
choiceExplanations: Reserving both brakes for emergencies is the habit the manual is written to prevent.
Both brakes are used on slippery surfaces too, with gentle, gradual pressure.
Load changes braking distance but does not change which brakes you use.

question: Why does the manual insist on using both brakes even for routine stops?
choices: So the skill is developed and automatic when an emergency comes
Because using one brake wears the pads unevenly
Because the rear brake alone is illegal on public roads
Because the front brake overheats if used alone
explanation: The reason is skill, not mechanics: using both brakes for even normal stops will permit you to develop the proper skill of using both brakes properly in an emergency. A rider who only ever uses the rear will reach for the rear under pressure, which is the pattern behind most crash-involved braking errors.
choiceExplanations: Pad wear is not the manual's reason; skill development is.
The manual states no such legal requirement about brake use.
No overheating warning is given for the front brake.

question: Of a motorcycle's total stopping power, roughly how much is available at the front brake?

Roughly a quarter of it
Roughly half of it
An equal share with the rear brake
explanation: The manual states that the front brake is more powerful and can provide 70% or more of your total stopping power, and that it is safe to use if you use it properly. Weight transferring forward under braking is what gives the front tire that extra traction.
choiceExplanations: A quarter badly understates the front brake and is the belief behind under-braking the front.
Half is still an understatement; the manual's figure is 70% or more.
The front is the more powerful of the two, not an equal partner with the rear.

question: How should the front brake be applied for a firm stop?

Grabbed hard at once to use all available traction
Applied in short repeated pulses
Applied only after the rear brake has locked

As weight transfers forward more traction becomes available at the front wheel, so the front brake can be applied more firmly after braking begins.
choiceExplanations: The manual warns not to grab the brake lever or use abrupt pressure — that is what locks the wheel.
Pulsing is what ABS does electronically; a rider squeezes progressively instead.
Locking the rear on purpose gives up directional control and is not a braking technique.

question: Maximum straight-line braking is achieved by:
choices: Fully applying both front and rear brakes without locking either wheel
Applying the front brake only, as hard as possible
Locking the rear wheel and steering with the front
Downshifting through every gear while braking lightly
explanation: The manual defines maximum straight-line braking as fully applying both front and rear brakes without locking either wheel. Keep your knees against the tank and your eyes up, looking well ahead, which helps you stop in a straight line and keeps lean angle out of the equation.

A locked rear wheel removes your ability to change direction and risks a high-side crash.
Engine braking supplements the brakes; it is not how maximum braking is produced.

question: During a maximum-effort stop, what should happen to rear brake pressure as the motorcycle slows?

It should increase steadily to match the front
It should be released entirely once the front is applied
It should be pulsed on and off about once a second

question: What happens to the traction available for braking when the motorcycle is leaned over?

It is unchanged, since the same tires are on the same road
It increases, because more of the tire is in contact with the road
It is reduced at the front only, not the rear
explanation: The manual states that any time a motorcycle is leaned over, the amount of traction available for braking is reduced, and the greater the lean angle, the more the possibility of the tires losing traction. Traction spent holding the corner is not available to stop you.
choiceExplanations: Lean angle changes how much of the tire's grip is being spent on cornering rather than stopping.
Contact patch area is not the governing factor; traction is being used for cornering instead.
The reduction applies to the motorcycle's traction generally, not to one wheel.

question: You must stop as quickly as possible while in a curve and conditions allow it. What does the manual say to do first?

Brake hard immediately and correct the lean afterwards
Widen your line into the next lane to reduce lean angle
Downshift to first gear before touching the brakes
explanation: The manual says that to stop as quickly and as safely as possible in a curve, and depending on road and traffic conditions, try to get the motorcycle as perpendicular to the road as possible, then brake. Standing it up restores the traction that lean angle was consuming.
choiceExplanations: Hard braking at full lean is exactly what the reduced traction cannot support.
Crossing into another lane trades a braking problem for a collision risk.
Aggressive downshifting adds a rear-wheel skid risk and does not restore braking traction.

question: What is an anti-lock braking system designed to do?
choices: Prevent wheel lock-up and avoid skids when stopping in panic situations
Shorten stopping distance on every surface by about half
Apply the front brake automatically when the rear is used
Keep the motorcycle upright during a swerve
explanation: The manual states that ABS is designed to prevent wheel lock-up and avoid skids when stopping in panic situations. It operates when too much pressure is applied to either brake control, releasing and reapplying pressure to maintain maximum braking effectiveness while the controls remain applied.
choiceExplanations: The manual claims no fixed reduction in stopping distance for ABS.
That describes an integrated braking system, which is a different mechanism.
ABS acts on braking; it does not stabilise the motorcycle during a swerve.

question: How quickly can an ABS release and reapply brake pressure?

About twice per second
About 5 times per second
About 50 times per second
explanation: The manual states that ABS is capable of releasing and reapplying pressure more than 15 times per second. That is far faster than a rider can modulate a lever, which is why the correct technique with ABS is to keep the brake controls applied rather than pumping them.
choiceExplanations: Twice a second is far slower than the manual's figure.
Five times per second understates the stated capability.
Fifty times per second overstates it; the manual says more than 15.

question: Which description matches an integrated braking system?

Both brakes release automatically when a wheel locks
The rear brake is disabled above a set speed
Braking force is shared equally between the wheels at all times
explanation: The manual describes linked braking as connecting the front and rear brakes so that either control applies pressure to both, and defines an integrated braking system as a variation of the linked system in which partial front braking is applied whenever the rear brake is activated.

No system described in the manual disables a brake at speed.
A linked system applies both brakes from either control, but not with equal force by definition.

question: What are the four steps of a turn, in order?
choices: SLOW, LOOK, PRESS, ROLL
LOOK, SLOW, ROLL, PRESS
PRESS, SLOW, LOOK, ROLL
SLOW, PRESS, ROLL, LOOK
explanation: The manual's four steps are SLOW, LOOK, PRESS and ROLL. Reduce speed before the turn, look through the turn to where you want to go, press the handgrip to lean the motorcycle, then roll on the throttle to maintain or slightly increase speed. In practice the steps overlap, but the order is the point.
choiceExplanations: Speed must come off before the turn; looking through it comes after slowing.
Pressing to lean before slowing means entering the corner too fast, the classic error.
Looking through the turn belongs before the lean, not after the throttle is rolled on.

question: In the LOOK step, what exactly should you turn?

Your head and shoulders together
Your whole upper body into the corner
Your eyes only, keeping your head straight ahead
explanation: The manual's LOOK step says to look through the turn to where you want to go, turning just your head, not your shoulders, and keeping your eyes level with the horizon. Where you look is where the motorcycle goes, so looking at the exit rather than at the edge of the road is what keeps your line.
choiceExplanations: The manual says to turn just your head, not your shoulders.
Turning the upper body changes your weight on the motorcycle and is not what is instructed.
Eyes alone limit how far through the turn you can see; the head turns with them.

Press the right handgrip so the motorcycle leans left
Pull the left handgrip toward you
Shift your weight left without touching the handgrips
explanation: The manual states that to turn, the motorcycle must lean, and that to lean it you press on the handgrip in the direction of the turn: press left handgrip, lean left, go left. The higher the speed or the sharper the turn, the greater the lean angle needs to be.
choiceExplanations: Pressing the right handgrip leans the motorcycle right and takes you right.

The left handgrip, to counter-balance the motorcycle right
Both handgrips equally, to keep the motorcycle upright
Neither — they lean their body right instead

Pressing both equally produces no lean and therefore no change of direction.
Body lean alone is not the manual's swerve technique; hand pressure on the handgrip is.

Lean with the motorcycle at the same angle
Lean the body further than the motorcycle
Keep the motorcycle upright and steer with the handlebars alone

choiceExplanations: Leaning together at the same angle is what you do in regular turns, not slow tight ones.

The motorcycle must lean to turn; keeping it upright is not an option in a tight turn.

A U-turn at walking pace
Manoeuvring the motorcycle at idle

At the apex of the turn
As the motorcycle begins to lean
Immediately after the lean angle is greatest
explanation: The manual says it is best to change gears before entering a turn, and that if shifting in the turn is necessary you must do it smoothly, because a sudden change in power to the rear wheel can cause a skid. Gear selection belongs with the SLOW step, not with the lean.

Path 1, the left third
Path 3, the right third
Whichever path is closest to the shoulder

Path 3, closest to the parked cars, so drivers can see you
Path 2 only, regardless of where the hazards are

question: You are following a van on a wet road at night. What following distance does the manual point to?
choices: Three seconds or more
Two seconds, the standard minimum
One second, since the van's brake lights are easy to see
Whatever gap keeps the van's tail lights in view
explanation: Three of the manual's triggers apply at once here: the pavement is slippery, you cannot see through the vehicle ahead, and it is night, when the manual separately says to open up a three-second following distance or more. Each on its own would justify more than two seconds.
choiceExplanations: Two seconds is the normal minimum; this situation stacks three separate reasons to exceed it.
A short gap removes any room to stop, and brake lights do not create stopping distance.
Keeping tail lights in view is not a measure of stopping distance at all.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Keeping Your Distance
source.sourceQuote: open up a three-second or more following distance

question: How do you check your following distance using a marker on the road?
choices: Count 'one-thousand-one, one-thousand-two' from when the vehicle ahead passes it
Count the number of dashed lane markings between you and the vehicle ahead
Estimate the gap in motorcycle lengths
Time how long the vehicle ahead takes to reach the marker
explanation: The manual's method is to pick a marker such as a pavement marking or lamppost, and when the rear of the vehicle ahead passes it, count off the seconds. If you reach the marker before you reach 'two', you are following too closely.
choiceExplanations: Counting lane markings measures distance, not the time gap the manual uses.
Vehicle lengths are not the measure; the manual counts seconds.
You time yourself reaching the marker after the vehicle ahead, not the vehicle's own approach.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Keeping Your Distance
source.sourceQuote: If you reach the marker before you reach “two,” you are following too closely.

question: You count 'one-thousand-one' and reach the marker. What does that tell you?
choices: You are following too closely and should drop back
You are at a safe two-second distance
You have a three-second cushion
Nothing useful — the count only works above 40 mph
explanation: The rule is that if you reach the marker before you reach 'two', you are following too closely. Arriving on the count of one is about a one-second gap — half the normal minimum — and leaves almost nothing with which to stop or swerve.
choiceExplanations: Reaching the marker at 'one' is roughly a one-second gap, half the stated minimum.
A three-second cushion would mean reaching the marker after the full count of three.
The manual applies the counting method without any speed qualification.

question: What is the manual's recommended way to deal with someone following you too closely?
choices: Get them in front of you — let them pass, or slow and open space ahead
Speed up until they fall back
Brake sharply to warn them off
Move to the edge of the lane and maintain speed
explanation: The manual says a better way to handle tailgaters is to get them in front of you: when someone is following too closely, try to let them pass. If you cannot, slow down and open up extra space ahead to allow room for both you and the tailgater to stop, which also encourages them to pass.
choiceExplanations: The manual warns this can simply produce a tailgater at a higher speed.
Sharp braking in front of a tailgater invites the rear-end collision you are trying to avoid.
Moving to the lane edge does not remove the tailgater and gives up your space cushion.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Keeping Your Distance
source.sourceQuote: A better way to handle tailgaters is to get them in front of you.

question: Why does the manual reject speeding up to shake off a tailgater?
choices: It can end up with someone tailgating you at a higher speed
It is illegal to exceed the speed limit to avoid a tailgater
It uses more fuel than slowing down
It makes your brake light harder to see
explanation: The manual's reasoning is that speeding up to lose someone following too closely can end up with someone tailgating you at a higher speed. The problem has not been solved, only made faster. Getting them in front of you removes it entirely.
choiceExplanations: The manual's objection is practical, not a statement about the speed limit.
Fuel use is nowhere part of the manual's reasoning.
Brake light visibility is discussed separately and is not affected by your speed.

question: Where should you ride before beginning a pass?
choices: In the left portion of your lane at a safe following distance
In the right portion of your lane to leave room to pull out
Directly behind the vehicle's bumper for the shortest pass
Alongside the vehicle before signalling
explanation: The manual's first passing step is to ride in the left portion of the lane at a safe following distance to increase your line of sight and make you more visible. You then signal and check for oncoming traffic, using your mirrors and turning your head to check your blind spot.
choiceExplanations: The right portion narrows your line of sight past the vehicle ahead.
Closing right up removes your view ahead and your stopping distance.
Riding alongside before signalling puts you in the blind spot with no plan.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Keeping Your Distance
source.sourceQuote: Ride in the left portion of the lane at a safe following distance to increase your line of sight and make you more visible.

question: Which statement about passing does the manual NOT support?
choices: A pass may be completed above the posted limit if it shortens the time alongside
Do not linger in the blind spot
Signal again before returning to your original lane, then cancel the signal
Check your mirrors and turn your head before moving out
explanation: The manual states that passes must be completed within posted speed limits, and only where permitted. Nothing about shortening exposure alongside another vehicle licenses exceeding the limit; the other three statements are steps the manual gives.
choiceExplanations: This is correct — time spent in another driver's blind spot is time they cannot see you.
This is correct — the manual's fourth passing step is exactly this.
This is correct — mirrors plus a headcheck before moving out is the first step.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Keeping Your Distance
source.sourceQuote: passes must be completed within posted speed limits, and only where permitted

question: When another vehicle is passing you from behind, where should you ride?
choices: In the centre portion of your lane
In the portion of the lane closest to the passing vehicle
On the shoulder until the pass is complete
As far right as possible, regardless of the passing side
explanation: The manual says that when you are being passed from behind, stay in the centre portion of your lane, because riding close to the passing vehicle could put you in a hazardous situation. The four hazards it names are a sideswipe, extended mirrors, objects thrown from windows, and blasts of wind from larger vehicles.
choiceExplanations: Riding close to the passing vehicle exposes you to extended mirrors, sideswipes and windblast.
Leaving the road surface for a routine pass introduces a loose-surface hazard for no gain.
Hugging one edge gives up your cushion and may put you on debris at the lane edge.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Keeping Your Distance
source.sourceQuote: When you are being passed from behind, stay in the center portion of your lane.

question: A large truck is overtaking you on a windy day. What does the manual say about your position?
choices: Being in the farther portion of the lane gives you more room for error when the windblast hits
Move closer to the truck so the blast passes over you
Accelerate to match the truck's speed until it moves ahead
Pull onto the shoulder and stop until it has passed
explanation: The manual lists blasts of wind from larger vehicles among the hazards of being passed, and says you have more room for error if you are in the farther portion when hit by this blast than if you are closer to their lane. Staying in the centre portion of your own lane is the position it recommends.
choiceExplanations: Moving closer increases exposure to the blast, to extended mirrors and to a sideswipe.
Matching speed keeps you alongside in the blind spot for longer, which the manual warns against.
Stopping on the shoulder for a routine overtake creates its own hazard and is not advised.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Keeping Your Distance

question: What does the manual say about lane sharing?
choices: Cars and motorcycles need a full lane to operate safely, and lane sharing is usually prohibited
Lane sharing is safe provided both vehicles are moving slowly
Lane sharing is permitted when traffic is stopped
Lane sharing is encouraged in heavy traffic to reduce congestion
explanation: The manual states that cars and motorcycles need a full lane to operate safely, and that lane sharing is usually prohibited. Riding between rows of stopped or moving cars in the same lane leaves you vulnerable to a hand out of a window, a door opening, or a car turning suddenly.
choiceExplanations: Low speed does not remove the hazards: a door could open or a car could turn suddenly.
The manual gives no stopped-traffic exception; it warns specifically about rows of stopped cars.
The manual discourages lane sharing rather than encouraging it.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Keeping Your Distance
source.sourceQuote: Cars and motorcycles need a full lane to operate safely. Lane sharing is usually prohibited.

question: Drivers are most tempted to squeeze past you in the same lane in which situation?
choices: Heavy, bumper-to-bumper traffic
On an open rural road at speed
When you are riding in the left portion of the lane on a motorway
When your headlight is on during the day
explanation: The manual lists the situations where drivers are most tempted to squeeze by: in heavy, bumper-to-bumper traffic, when they want to pass you, when you are preparing to turn at an intersection, and when you are moving into an exit lane or leaving a highway. Keeping a centre-portion position discourages it.
choiceExplanations: Open roads with space to overtake properly are not where drivers try to share a lane.
Lane position can discourage sharing, but the temptation the manual names is heavy traffic.
A daytime headlight increases your conspicuity; it does not invite lane sharing.

question: A driver is coming down an entrance ramp onto the highway ahead of you. What does the manual advise?
choices: Give them plenty of room — change lanes if one is open, or adjust speed to open space
Hold your speed and lane so the merging driver can predict you
Speed up to clear the merge point before they arrive
Move to the lane edge nearest the ramp so they can see you
explanation: The manual says drivers on an entrance ramp may not see you on the highway, so give them plenty of room. Change to another lane if one is open; if there is no room for a lane change, adjust speed to open up space for the merging vehicle.
choiceExplanations: Predictability does not help a driver who has not seen you at all, which is the stated problem.
Racing a merging vehicle to the same point is the opposite of creating a space cushion.
Moving toward the ramp reduces your escape room instead of increasing it.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c

source.sourceQuote: Drivers on an entrance ramp may not see you on the highway. Give them plenty of room.

question: Why does the manual tell you not to ride next to cars or trucks in other lanes?
choices: You may be in a blind spot, and vehicles alongside block your escape from danger ahead
It makes it harder for you to see traffic signals
It increases fuel consumption from wind turbulence
It is prohibited on multi-lane highways
explanation: The manual gives two reasons together: you might be in the blind spot and a vehicle could switch into your lane without warning, and vehicles in the next lane also block your escape if you come upon danger in your own lane. Its advice is to speed up or drop back to find a place clear of traffic on both sides.
choiceExplanations: Signal visibility is not the reason the manual gives for avoiding positions alongside vehicles.
Fuel use is never part of the manual's safety reasoning.
The manual gives a safety reason, not a legal prohibition, for avoiding this position.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Keeping Your Distance
source.sourceQuote: Do not ride next to cars or trucks in other lanes if you do not have to.

question: Why does the manual say to keep well behind the vehicle ahead even when you are stopped?
choices: So you can get out of the way if someone bears down on you from behind
So your headlight does not dazzle the driver ahead
So the engine does not overheat in traffic
Because stopping closer is prohibited at traffic signals
explanation: The manual says keeping well behind the vehicle ahead even when stopped makes it easier to get out of the way if someone bears down on you from behind, and gives you a cushion if the vehicle ahead starts to back up. A stopped motorcycle with no space in front of it has nowhere to go.
choiceExplanations: Dazzle is not the manual's concern here; escape room is.
Engine temperature is not among the reasons the manual gives.
No legal stopping distance at signals is stated in the manual.

source.chapterTitle: Ride Within Your Abilities - Keeping Your Distance

question: Where should you ride so the driver ahead can see you in their inside rearview mirror?
choices: The centre portion of the lane
The far left of the lane
The far right of the lane
Directly in the driver's left blind spot
explanation: The manual says that when behind a car, ride where the driver can see you in the inside rearview mirror, and that riding in the centre portion of the lane should put you in view. Riding at the far side of a lane may only put you in a sideview mirror, which most drivers check far less often.
choiceExplanations: The far side of a lane may only show you in a sideview mirror, which drivers check far less often.
The same problem applies on the right: sideview mirrors get much less attention.
A blind spot is by definition where the driver cannot see you at all.

question: What do the three letters of SEE stand for?
choices: Search, Evaluate, Execute
Scan, Estimate, Escape
Slow, Evaluate, Exit
See, Expect, Escape
explanation: The manual describes SEE as the MSF's three-step strategy: Search, Evaluate, Execute. It exists to help you assess what is going on in traffic so you can plan and implement the safest course of action as traffic situations change.
choiceExplanations: Scan and estimate are plausible words, but the manual's three steps are search, evaluate and execute.
SLOW is the first step of a turn, not of the SEE strategy.
The strategy is not a description of expectations; its final step is a physical action.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: They reduce their risk by using MSF's three-step SEE strategy

question: What is the purpose of the SEE strategy?
choices: To assess traffic so you can plan and carry out the safest course of action as situations change
To pass the on-cycle skills test
To keep the motorcycle stable in corners
To decide which lane position is legal
explanation: The manual says SEE will help you assess what is going on in traffic so you can plan and implement the safest course of action as traffic situations change. It is the reasoning layer behind the specific rules, which is why it applies to situations the manual never lists.
choiceExplanations: The skills test measures physical control; SEE is a mental strategy for traffic.
Cornering stability is handled by the four steps of a turn, not by SEE.
Lane position is a tool SEE uses, but legality is not what the strategy decides.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c

question: When searching, what does the manual tell you to focus on finding?
choices: Potential escape paths
The speed limit signs
Other motorcyclists
Police vehicles
explanation: The manual says that as you search, focus on finding potential escape paths, especially in or around intersections, shopping areas and school and construction zones. An escape path is what converts a surprise into a manoeuvre instead of a collision.
choiceExplanations: Speed limits matter, but the search is about where you could go if something goes wrong.
Other riders are not the object of the search strategy.
Enforcement is irrelevant to the manual's search priorities.

source.sourceQuote: As you search, focus on finding potential escape paths, especially in or around intersections, shopping areas and school and construction zones.

question: Which areas does the manual single out as needing the most assertive searching?
choices: Intersections, shopping areas, and school and construction zones
Interstate highways and toll plazas
Rural two-lane roads at night
Residential streets with parked cars
explanation: The manual names intersections, shopping areas, and school and construction zones both as search priorities and, later, as the potential high-risk areas where you should cover the clutch and both brakes to reduce the time you need to react.
choiceExplanations: Highways are not the manual's named high-risk search areas; conflict points are.
Night riding gets its own advice, but these are not the named searching priorities.
Parked cars are covered separately; the named areas are intersections and busy zones.

source.sourceQuote: As you search, focus on finding potential escape paths, especially in or around intersections, shopping areas and school and construction zones.

question: How far ahead is the manual's long search distance, expressed in time?
choices: About 12 seconds
About 4 seconds
About 2 seconds
About 30 seconds
explanation: The manual says to search for hazards that are further out, looking ahead to an area it would take about 12 seconds to reach. That distance provides time to prepare for a situation before it becomes urgent, which the shorter lead times cannot do.
choiceExplanations: Four seconds defines the immediate path, not the long search.
Two seconds is the minimum following distance behind the vehicle ahead.
Thirty seconds is not a figure the manual uses.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: search for hazards that are further out, looking ahead to an area it would take about 12 seconds to reach

question: Anything within how many seconds of your path is considered immediate?
choices: 4 seconds
2 seconds
8 seconds
12 seconds
explanation: The manual states that anything within 4 seconds of your path is considered immediate, because 4 seconds can provide enough time and space to swerve and/or brake for fixed hazards or for someone or something entering your path.
choiceExplanations: Two seconds is the minimum following distance, not the immediate hazard zone.
Eight seconds is not one of the manual's three lead times.
Twelve seconds is the long search area, which exists precisely so hazards are not yet immediate.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: Anything that is within 4 seconds of your path is considered immediate

question: Which of the manual's three lead times is the minimum following distance?
choices: 2 seconds
4 seconds
12 seconds
1 second
explanation: The manual lists three lead times and begins with the closest: first, have at least a 2-second following distance. The 4-second immediate path and the 12-second search area extend outward from there.
choiceExplanations: Four seconds describes the immediate path around you, not the gap you keep behind a vehicle.
Twelve seconds is the long search area well ahead of you.
One second is not a lead time the manual uses at all.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: First, have at least a 2-second following distance.

question: A rider keeps a good gap behind the car ahead but never looks beyond it. Which part of the search are they missing?
choices: The 12-second look that lets them prepare before a situation becomes urgent
The 2-second following distance
The mirror check behind them
The lean-angle assessment for the next curve
explanation: The manual's point in giving three lead times is that they do different jobs. A 2-second gap handles the vehicle in front. Only the search to an area about 12 seconds ahead provides time to prepare for a situation before it becomes urgent, and that is exactly what this rider has given up.
choiceExplanations: A good gap behind the car ahead is the 2-second distance, which they already have.
Mirror checks are part of searching behind, which is a separate omission from the one described.
Lean angle is a control matter, not one of the search lead times.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: search for hazards that are further out, looking ahead to an area it would take about 12 seconds to reach

question: What does the Evaluate step ask you to do?
choices: Think about how hazards can interact to create risks for you
Estimate your stopping distance at the current speed
Judge whether other drivers have seen you
Decide whether the road surface is legal to ride on
explanation: The manual defines it directly: evaluate means to think about how hazards can interact to create risks for you. It then tells you to anticipate potential problems and have a plan to reduce risks, considering road and surface characteristics, traffic control devices, other vehicles, and available escape paths.
choiceExplanations: Stopping distance is one input, but Evaluate is about how hazards combine into risk.
The manual says never to count on eye contact, so judging whether you were seen is not the task.
Road surfaces are evaluated for traction, not for legality.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: Evaluate means to think about how hazards can interact to create risks for you.

question: Which of these is NOT one of the things the manual tells you to evaluate?
choices: The registration status of vehicles around you
Road and surface characteristics such as potholes and guardrails
Traffic control devices including signals, warning signs and pavement markings
Escape paths, in front or to the sides
explanation: The manual's Evaluate list covers road and surface characteristics, traffic control devices, vehicles and other traffic that may move into your path, and escape paths. Nothing about other vehicles' paperwork appears, and nothing in it would help you predict what they do next.
choiceExplanations: This is on the manual's list — surface features shape your riding strategy.
This is on the list — traffic control devices require you to evaluate circumstances ahead.
This is on the list — escape paths need to be available, in front or to the sides.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: Evaluate means to think about how hazards can interact to create risks for you.

question: How does the manual say the Execute step should be carried out?
choices: With smoothness and precision
As quickly as possible, whatever it takes
Only after the hazard has clearly committed
By braking first in every case
explanation: The manual says to execute your decision with smoothness and precision. The three actions available are communicating your presence with lights and/or horn, adjusting your speed by accelerating, stopping or slowing, and adjusting your position or direction by swerving, changing lanes, or moving within your lane.
choiceExplanations: Abrupt inputs cause skids; the manual asks for smooth, precise action rather than raw speed.
Waiting for a hazard to commit removes the time and space that make a response possible.
Braking is one of three tools; sometimes the answer is to accelerate or change position.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: Execute your decision with smoothness and precision.

question: Which of these is one of the three ways the manual says to execute a decision?
choices: Communicating your presence with lights and/or horn
Signalling to other riders with hand signals
Sounding the horn continuously until the hazard clears
Stopping in the traffic lane until the situation resolves
explanation: The manual's Execute actions are: communicating your presence with lights and/or horn, adjusting your speed, and adjusting your position and/or direction. Communicating is first because it can remove the hazard before any evasive action is needed.
choiceExplanations: Hand signals are a group-riding tool, not one of the three Execute actions.
The manual says to sound the horn loud and long in an emergency, but continuous use is not the strategy.
Stopping in a live lane creates a new hazard rather than executing a decision.

source.sourceDocument: West Virginia Motorcycle Operator Manual, 18th edition (Motorcycle Safety Foundation), retrieved 2026-09-15, SHA-256 3153bb43aa19c5037198e63dab8b764f2c4042118e1e0b3cae4f1c263ba7148c
source.sourceQuote: Communicating  your presence with lights and/or horn.

question: Two hazards are developing at once. What does the manual advise?
choices: Adjust speed to let them separate, then deal with them one at a time
Deal with the nearer one and accept the risk from the other
Split the difference and pass between them
Brake to a stop until both have cleared
explanation: The manual applies the old adage 'one step at a time' to two or more hazards: adjust speed to permit two hazards to separate, then deal with them one at a time as single hazards. Decision-making becomes more complex with three or more, where you evaluate the consequences of each and give equal distance to the hazards.
choiceExplanations: Ignoring one hazard abandons the evaluation instead of resolving it.
Splitting the difference gives equal exposure to both rather than separating them in time.
Stopping in traffic is not the manual's answer; adjusting speed to separate hazards is.

question: In potential high-risk areas such as intersections and school zones, what does the manual tell you to cover?
choices: The clutch and both brakes
The horn button only
The clutch only
The rear brake only
explanation: The manual says that in potential high-risk areas, such as intersections, shopping areas, and school and construction zones, cover the clutch and both brakes to reduce the time you need to react. It repeats the same instruction in the intersections section.
choiceExplanations: The horn is one Execute tool, but covering it does not reduce braking reaction time.
Covering the clutch alone leaves the brakes an extra movement away.
The rear brake alone provides under a third of stopping power; both brakes are covered.

question: What does the manual call the habit of aggressively scanning ahead, to the sides and behind?

Running a T-CLOCS sweep
Counterbalancing
A staggered scan
explanation: The manual describes using your 'RiderRadar' to aggressively scan the environment ahead of you, to the sides, and behind you to avoid potential hazards even before they arise. It is the active, searching-out form of looking that the Search step calls for.
choiceExplanations: T-CLOCS is the pre-ride inspection checklist, not a scanning habit.
Counterbalancing is a body-position technique for slow, tight turns.
Staggered formation is a group-riding spacing pattern.

question: What proportion of motorcycle/car crashes does the manual attribute to drivers violating a rider's right-of-way?

About one-quarter
About one-tenth
Nearly all of them
explanation: The manual states that over one-half of motorcycle/car crashes are caused by drivers violating a rider's right-of-way. That is why it treats intersections as the greatest potential for conflict between you and other traffic.
choiceExplanations: One-quarter badly understates the figure the manual gives.
One-tenth is far below the manual's figure.
The manual says over one-half, not almost all — riders also contribute to crashes.

question: Which vehicle movement does the manual identify as the biggest danger at intersections?
choices: Cars turning left in front of you
Cars following you too closely through the junction
Cars stopping suddenly ahead of you
Cars overtaking you as you enter the junction
explanation: The manual names cars that turn left in front of you — including cars turning left from the lane on your right — and cars on side streets that pull into your lane as the biggest dangers. The left-turning car across your path is the classic motorcycle crash.
choiceExplanations: Tailgaters are a hazard, but they are not the manual's named intersection danger.
Sudden stops ahead are a following-distance problem, not the intersection danger named here.
Being overtaken has its own guidance and is not the biggest intersection danger.

question: According to the manual, what counts as an intersection?
choices: Anywhere traffic may cross your path of travel, including a residential driveway
Only junctions controlled by a signal or a stop sign
Only the crossing of two or more numbered roads
Only places where lanes of traffic physically merge
explanation: The manual says an intersection can be in the middle of an urban area or at a driveway on a residential street — anywhere traffic may cross your path of travel. A driveway with no markings and no signs is still an intersection for the purpose of the strategy.
choiceExplanations: Control devices do not define an intersection; crossing paths do.
Road classification has nothing to do with the manual's definition.
Merging is a separate situation with its own guidance.

question: A driver waiting to pull out appears to look directly at you. What does the manual say this means?
choices: Nothing reliable — a driver can look right at a rider and still fail to see them
You have been seen and may proceed at your normal speed
The driver has yielded the right-of-way to you
You should accelerate to clear the junction before they move
explanation: The manual is unambiguous: there are no guarantees that others see you, and you should never count on eye contact, because too often a driver looks right at a motorcyclist and still fails to see him or her. The only eyes you can count on are your own.
choiceExplanations: The manual says there are no guarantees that others see you, so this is not a safe conclusion.
Looking at you is not yielding, and nothing has been communicated.
Accelerating removes your options if the driver does pull out; the manual says to slow and cover the controls.

question: What assumption does the manual tell you to make about a car that could enter your path?
choices: Assume that it will
Assume it will yield if you have the green
Assume it will see your headlight
Assume it will stop at the line
explanation: The manual's rule is blunt: if a car can enter your path, assume that it will. It adds that good riders are always 'looking for trouble' — not to get into it, but to stay out of it.
choiceExplanations: Having the right-of-way does not stop a driver who violates it — that is most of these crashes.
A daytime headlight helps, but the manual never treats being seen as guaranteed.
Cars on side streets pulling into your lane are one of the two biggest dangers named.

question: Approaching an intersection where a driver is preparing to cross your path, what should you cover?
choices: The clutch lever and both brakes
The horn and the front brake
The clutch only
The rear brake only
explanation: The manual says to cover the clutch lever and both brakes to reduce reaction time. Covering the controls removes the time it would otherwise take to find them, which is the difference between stopping short and not.
choiceExplanations: The horn is useful but covering it does nothing for your braking reaction time.
Covering the clutch alone leaves both brakes a hand and foot movement away.
The rear brake supplies under a third of stopping power; both brakes are covered.

question: Which action does the manual recommend when approaching an intersection where a vehicle may cross your path?
choices: Slow and select a lane position that increases your visibility to that driver
Speed up to shorten the time you are exposed
Move as far right as possible to stay out of the way
Hold your speed and position so the driver can judge you accurately
explanation: The manual says that when approaching an intersection where a vehicle driver is preparing to cross your path, slow and select a lane position to increase your visibility to that driver, then cover the clutch lever and both brakes. As you enter, move away from the vehicle.
choiceExplanations: Speeding up reduces the time and space you have if the driver does pull out.
The right edge may hide you behind other traffic and removes your escape path.
Holding position assumes the driver has seen you, which the manual says you cannot assume.

question: Why does the manual warn against changing speed or position radically at an intersection?
choices: Drivers might think you are preparing to turn
It uses up traction you may need for braking
It makes your headlight harder to see
It is prohibited within 100 feet of a junction
explanation: The manual says not to change speed or position radically, as drivers might think you are preparing to turn. Lane position is one of the ways a rider communicates intentions, so a large sudden movement sends a message you did not intend to send.
choiceExplanations: Traction loss is a cornering and braking concern, not the reason given here.
Headlight visibility does not change with speed or lane position adjustments.
No such distance rule appears in the manual.

question: An oncoming vehicle is signalling a left turn in the middle of a block, nowhere near an intersection. What does the manual advise?
choices: Use the same intersection strategy — slow, position for visibility, cover the controls
Ignore it, since the strategy only applies at intersections
Accelerate past before the vehicle can turn
Move to the right edge of your lane and maintain speed
explanation: The manual closes the intersection strategy with this extension: this strategy should also be used whenever a vehicle in the oncoming lane of traffic is signaling for a left turn, whether at an intersection or not. A driveway mid-block produces the same crash as a junction.
choiceExplanations: The manual expressly extends the strategy beyond intersections for exactly this situation.
Accelerating shortens your own reaction time and options if the vehicle turns.
Maintaining speed at the lane edge gives up both visibility and escape room.

question: Approaching a blind intersection, which part of the lane should you move to?
choices: The portion that brings you into the other driver's field of vision earliest
The portion nearest the kerb, to leave room to stop
The centre, regardless of where the obstruction is
The portion closest to the obstruction, to see around it sooner
explanation: The manual says that if you approach a blind intersection, move to the portion of the lane that will bring you into another driver's field of vision at the earliest possible moment. In its own illustration the rider moves to the left portion of the lane — away from the parked car — so the driver on the cross street can see him earlier.
choiceExplanations: Hugging the kerb usually hides you behind the very thing blocking the view.
A fixed centre position ignores which side the sight line is blocked on.
Moving toward the obstruction delays both your view out and the driver's view of you.
